Gavi Gaṅgādhareśvara Temple
------------------------------------------
This is an ancient temple of Lord शिव, situated in a natural cave. It is located in the south-west part of Bangalore city (now Beṅgaḷūru), the capital of Karnataka State.
According to the local legends, it belongs to the त्रेतायुग, the second of the four युगस्. The two well-known sages गौतम and Bhāradvāja used to worship here.
The original stone temple might have been built during the reign of the पल्लवस् (A.

-900).
It is said to have been accidentally discovered by Kempe Gowda (17th century A. D.) the then chieftain of Bangalore, in A.

. The present structure is the one renovated by him.
The temple which covers an area of 92 meters (300 ft.) by 61 meters (200 ft.), can be divided into three parts: the outer courtyard, the inner hall and the cave shrine proper, in two parts.
The outer courtyard has two monolithic pillars with big circular discs at the top, called Sūryapāna and Candrapāna. There are two more such pillars with त्रिशूल (trident) and डमरु (small kettle- drum) at the top.
A ध्वजस्तम्भ (flagpost) has been erected facing the image.
The inner hall which has 14 pillars, contains a small shrine for सुब्रह्मण्य with his two consorts (Vaḷḷī and Devayānī), नवग्रहस् (the nine प्लनेत्स्) and आञ्जनेय.
In the outer part of the inner cave, there are shrines for गणेश, पार्वती and दुर्गा.
Other images are those of अग्नि (the fire-god), वीरभद्र (an aspect of शिव), and सप्तमातृकास् (the Seven-Mothers, attendants of दुर्गा).
There are three cave-paths round the main shrine. The first is well-lighted and one can go round it. It contains the images of the sages गौतम and Bhāradvāja as also Caṇḍikeśvara, Śaṇmukha, दक्षिणा-mūrti, कालभैरव and शक्ति-गणपति.
The second path which is situated next to the shrine of पार्वती is said to contain the cave where गौतम performed तपस् (austerities).
The third is believed to lead to काशी (Vārāṇasī) and Śivagaṅgā (a mountain with temples) near Bangalore. But it is inaccessible and hence nobody has dared to go through it.
The innermost part of the cave is the main sanctum, containing a medium-sized शिवलिङ्ग. Apart from the usual arrangement for dripping water over the लिङ्ग, it is also noticed that water drops through the rock over it during the rainy season.
One astronomical phenomenon that attracts a very large number of devotees every year happens on the मकर सङ्क्रान्ति day, which generally falls on the 14th of January. On this day, between 5 and 5.30 p.m., sunlight passes through the two windows on the western side of the temple, passes through the image of नन्दि and falls on the शिवलिङ्ग, thereby indicating the beginning of the उत्तरायण or change over of the sun’s movement from the south to the north.
Actually this phenomenon occurs for about 3 to 4 days (January 13 to 15).
According to a recent discovery, the sunlight falls on the शिवलिङ्ग during the period, November 26 to 30 also.
Another natural event that has been lately noticed is that the shadow of the ध्वजस्तम्भ (flagstaff) falls on the eastern pillar around the 22nd of June every year.
Mahāśivarātri (usually in February/ March) is the biggest festival of the year.
The रथोत्सव or temple-car festival is held on the paurṇamī (full-मोओन्) day of the month of Māgha (January/February) which draws a very large crowd of votaries.

Gavāmayana
(‘course of the cows [or rays of the sun]’)
------------------------------------------
The Vedic sacrifices—yajñas or yāgas—are an ancient institution. According to the Bhagavadgītā (3.10 and 11) sacrifices were created by प्रजापति (Lord of men, the creator) himself at the very beginning of च्रेअतिओन्.
Among the various varieties of such sacrifices, the सत्त्रयाग is also one. It is the one sacrifice wherein all the priests who perform it are also the yajamānas (masters who reap the results equally). The duration of a सत्त्रयाग may be from 12 days up to a year or more. The गवामयन is a typical सत्त्रयाग, a model for such sacrifices of one year’s duration. It may be performed for various rewards like progeny, prosperity, greatness or हेअवेन्.
The sacrifice is performed in three phases. The first and the third are spread over 180 days (6 lunar months of 30 days) each. In between comes the viṣuvat or the central day.
Several rites like अभिप्लव (a सोम ritual), अग्निष्टोम (a सोम sacrifice), Daśarātra (another rite of ten days’ duration) and Udayanīya (a concluding rite of any सोमयाग) are involved in this सत्त्रयाग.
See also VEDIC SACRIFICES.
